findings.excerpt: A fenced TikZ picture is opened on the same line as its \begin{tikzpicture} source; the subsequent \draw, \node, and closing command are shown literally.
findings.symptom: The screenshot prints the raw TikZ source as plain text in Remarks rather than showing the complementary forbidden-basis diagram.
findings.mathematical_check: The source code describes two isolated vertices labelled \bar K_2, a complement arrow, and two vertices joined by one edge labelled K_2. These are complementary graphs, so the map and edge content are correct; only the diagram block fails to render.
findings.suggested_repair: Move \begin{tikzpicture} to a new line after the tikz fence opener and retain the two graph panels and complement arrow.

findings.excerpt: The example identifies the upper-left 3×3 Durfee square of λ=(5,3,3,2,1), the two cells to its right as α=(2), and the cells below it as β=(2,1), but supplies no Young/Ferrers diagram.
findings.symptom: The text explains the square-and-arms decomposition by referring to cells on the right and below, while the screenshot contains only prose and formulas.
findings.mathematical_check: The row lengths (5,3,3,2,1) determine a 3×3 Durfee square; the remainder to the right is a row of length 2 and the remainder below has row lengths (2,1). A diagram can show those three regions without adding mathematical content.
findings.suggested_repair: Add a Ferrers/Young diagram with the 3×3 Durfee square distinguished, the right-hand α=(2) cells marked, and the lower β=(2,1) cells marked.
